Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:47: Regarding the mystery of the threads, which are thirty-two, it says that they correspond to the thirty-two paths of Chochmah, going out through the Righteous One (Tzaddik) — this being "from the wing of the earth we have heard songs, glory to the righteous one" (Isaiah 24:16). This does not contradict the earlier passages we quoted from Rashbi, which indicate that they are in Chayah, since the thirty-two paths go out from above through the Righteous One and spread out in Chayah, one to each side.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:48: And incidentally, it is proven there that one should not recite the Shema without tzitzit, in the manner they said in the Gemara (Berachot 14b) regarding one who recites the Shema without tefillin. In these words, on the end of the verse, "Woe is me, the treacherous have dealt treacherously..." (Isaiah 24:16): and when I look at the tekhelet and see a strap for whipping, a place of awe to be feared, I say, "Woe is me" — for people do not know how to take heed and consider for what they are punished, to deal falsely in this — "the treacherous have dealt treacherously" — for they recite the Shema without tzitzit, and the witnesses testify falsely; and these are the treacherous ones who deal falsely with themselves; "and with treachery the treacherous have dealt treacherously" — their garment without tzitzit is called "a garment of treachery" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:49: It is necessarily derived from the doubling of the verse, "the treacherous have dealt treacherously," and "with treachery the treacherous have dealt treacherously," that there are two aspects: one, whoever recites the Shema without tzitzit; and the second, whoever has no tzitzit on his garment even outside the time of reciting the Shema — for a person is obligated to wear tzitzit all day long. And they said in the Gemara (Pesachim 113b) that whoever has no tzitzit on his garment is like one under a ban, in these words: our Rabbis taught, eight are like those under a ban from Heaven, and these are: one who has no wife; one who has a wife but has no children from her and does not divorce her; one who has children and does not raise them to Torah study; one who has no tefillin on his head and arm, and no tzitzit on his garment, and no mezuzah on his doorpost; one who withholds shoes from his feet; and some say, also one who does not recline at a gathering for a mitzvah — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:50: It is impossible to exempt oneself from this by wearing tzitzit only during the time of prayer, for the time for tzitzit is all day, like tefillin and mezuzah; but because tefillin require a clean body, people have refrained from wearing them except at the time of prayer. The early Tannaim, peace be upon them — Rabbi Eliezer the Great was careful to wear them all day, even when he was ill, as is proven in Sanhedrin (68a), and likewise Rabbeinu HaKadosh (Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi), as is proven in Ketubot (104a). And in Shabbat, at the end of the chapter HaSho'el (153a), our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said — and these are the words of Rabbi Eliezer — another interpretation: "Let your garments always be white" (Ecclesiastes 9:8) — this refers to tzitzit; "and let your head lack no oil" — this refers to tefillin — so far his words. This shows that the obligation is for a person to wear tzitzit and tefillin all day.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:51: And so the practice has been to wear a small tallit (tallit katan) all day, and tefillin — whoever can maintain a clean body is obligated to wear them even outside the time of prayer, for they said that [one who does not] is like one under a ban; the reason being that he appears to be casting off the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:52: And in the Sifrei it says: beloved is Israel, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, surrounded with commandments — tefillin on their heads, tefillin on their arms, tzitzit on their garments, mezuzah on their doorposts; concerning them David said, "Seven times a day I praise You" (Psalms 119:164). He entered the bathhouse and saw himself naked, and said, "Woe is me, that I am naked of commandments!" But when he considered the matter of circumcision, he began to compose praise upon it, as it is said, "For the leader, upon the eighth" (Psalms 6:1) [an allusion to the eighth day of circumcision]. To what may this be compared? To a king of flesh and blood who said to his wife, "Adorn yourself with every kind of jewelry, so that you will be pleasing to me." So the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: be distinguished with commandments, so that you will be pleasing before Me. And so it says, "You are beautiful, my beloved, as Tirtzah" (Song of Songs 6:4) — you are beautiful to Me if you are pleasing (retzuyah) to Me — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:53: Regarding the greatness of tzitzit, it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Shelach 163b) that one who wears tzitzit becomes "whole" (tamim), and concerning him it is said, "You shall be whole" (Deuteronomy 18:13), in these words: in the same manner, a person who wears tzitzit is made whole every day — "tam" (whole) through the four corners properly arranged; "yam" (sea) through that tekhelet of the fish [tinted by] the seventy levels of the sea; the evil side, when it looks at this person, cannot harm him with an evil eye. And then he is "Tam-Yam," together with YHVH his God, literally, in one arrangement — she above and he below. Afterward she ascends among the supernal levels; so too this person afterward ascends, through the tefillin, among the supernal levels. Therefore, "You shall be whole with YHVH your God" — with Him truly, at one time, in one moment, she is arranged above and the person is arranged below — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:54: Further on the greatness of tzitzit, its special property is to draw the Shechinah to dwell with him, as it is written, "and they shall make for themselves tzitzit on the corners of their garments throughout their generations (ledorotam)" (Numbers 15:38) — as though it said "lediratam" (for their dwelling), as they expounded in the Tikkunim (22b) regarding "to observe the Sabbath throughout their generations" (Exodus 31:16) — see there, and we shall quote its wording below. And therefore they said, of blessed memory (Menachot 43b), that whoever is careful with the commandment of tzitzit merits to receive the presence of the Shechinah — it is written here ["and you shall see it"] and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:55: Regarding whether the wrapping in tzitzit precedes tefillin or not, there are clear proofs in the Zohar and the Tikkunim that wrapping in tzitzit over one's head precedes the tefillin. First, in the Zohar (Parashat Bamidbar 120b), it is explained there that there are four things in deed, and corresponding to them four in speech, and it says: the first is to purify oneself, meaning to relieve his body; afterward he should accept upon himself this yoke, to spread over his head the separateness of the mitzvah [tzitzit]; afterward he binds the knot of unification, which is the tefillin — what are tefillin? The tefillah of the head and of the hand, and so on — so far his words, as it pertains to us. And in the Tikkunim (130b), in these words: come and see, when a person wraps himself in the wrapping of the mitzvah, and puts on tefillin, and recites the Shema, he has thereby established for Him a throne through the wrapping of the mitzvah — and this has already been established, "and a throne shall be established in kindness" (Isaiah 16:5) — and through the tefillin he crowns Him; this is what is written, "bind your headdress (pe'ercha) upon you" (Ezekiel 24:17), and he calls Him who sits upon the throne he established for Him, "Hear, O Israel"; thus the Holy One, blessed be He, establishes for him, in that world, a throne and a crown — so far his words. A person does not fulfill his obligation properly by wearing a small tallit under his clothes to fulfill the words of these passages, but only by spreading the commandment of tzitzit over his head — this being what is called "wrapping" (atifah).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:56: Regarding the placement of the tallit, I have seen those who are precise about the tzitzit that first came to the side of the head, that they should always remain on the side of the head, since once they have merited being elevated, it is not fitting for them to descend from their status; and this is the practice of all Ashkenazim, and most of the people of Italy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:57: Regarding the intention of the blessing to wrap oneself in tzitzit, it is fitting to intend that the neshamah is the one wrapping itself in the light of this mitzvah, both below and above, so that the root of the neshamah, which is above, will likewise be wrapped in the light of this mitzvah, in aspects that will be explained. This is a general rule for every single mitzvah a person performs: he must intend that his neshamah, which is a part of God above, is being rectified and illuminated by the light of that mitzvah; and so too regarding tefillin.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:58: I heard from the mouth of my teacher, peace be upon him, that the intention of wrapping oneself in tzitzit relates to what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Bamidbar Rabbah 18:21), that "tzitzit" numerically equals the 613 commandments that are within the Shechinah, in her aspect clothed within the Throne and within Metatron, in whom lies the mystery of tzitzit. And according to the explanation that the intent of the wrapping is for the neshamah, one should intend that within one's neshamah there are two hundred forty-eight spiritual limbs and three hundred sixty-five spiritual sinews, and all of them shine through the commandment of tzitzit. And so it is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 227a), that the mystery of tzitzit is Metatron, in these words: Metatron [has] six levels to the Throne, which total six hundred; "tzitzit" [is spelled] with two yods, and if a yod is missing, then a chirik [vowel] takes its place — thus it totals, on every side, in the four corners of the tzitzit, together with the thirteen sections of the tzitzit, six hundred thirteen (613) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:59: And in the book Tola'at Ya'akov (Sod HaTzitzit), it is explained how the number 613 is found in the tzitzit, and it writes, in these words: this mitzvah is equal to all the commandments, since it is the primary stone comprising 613 precious stones and 32 paths, and each and every path divides into two — good and evil, "remember" and "observe," positive commandments and negative commandments — and behold, these are 64; and each is comprised of ten sefirot, giving 640; subtract from these the 27 letters of the Torah, and behold, these are the 613 commandments of the Torah. This is what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in the chapter HaTekhelet (Menachot 43b) on "and you shall see it and remember all the commandments of the Lord" (Numbers 15:39) — the commandment of tzitzit is equal to all the commandments together — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:60: There are many more matters in the hint of this mitzvah, and we have explained only what pertains to practice, regarding the intent of the blessing and the handling of the tzitzit, and what pertains to practice — that since their hint is 32, corresponding to the 32 paths, or as explained above, it is fitting to separate them, each one on its own, and likewise when handling them one should intend the mysteries hinted at.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:61: Regarding tefillin, we have already said that their mystery is for the purification of thoughts, and to draw down holiness, as they are called "holiness" in the language of our Rabbis, of blessed memory. And in the Midrash HaNe'elam (Parashat Chayei Sarah 129a) it says that concerning the mystery of tefillin it is said, "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" (Exodus 25:8), in these words: they arose and went, he and Rabbi Yeisa and Rabbi Chiya; they found Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon revealing mysteries of tefillin. They came before him and said, "With what is the master occupied?" He said to them, "I am saying the reason for tefillin, for fortunate is the person who wears tefillin and knows their reason." They said, "If it pleases the master, let him say something to us." He said, "I heard from my father that the Holy One, blessed be He, out of the great love He had for Israel, said to them to make Him a Tabernacle, in the manner of the supernal Chariot above, so that His dwelling would come to be among them — this is what is written, 'And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.' And I heard from my father that here the reason for tefillin is concealed in this verse."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:62: Come and see, in the manner above, a sanctuary was made in His holy Chariots, and afterward the Holy One, blessed be He, caused His dwelling to rest among them. In this same manner, the colleagues, masters of the Mishnah, alluded to the reason for tefillin, that this person become a model of the supernal chariots — a lower chariot, a supernal chariot — so that His kingship may come to him and cause His dwelling to rest upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:63: We have learned that there are supernal mysteries and their models within them, and there are three chariots as models of the supernal holy ones — mysteries of the three letters of the holy Names of the worlds, three chariots, three letters; four portions ruling over four; and concerning this is the mystery of the Shin with three crowns and the Shin with four crowns. Three kings rule over the body; the tefillin are upon it, the Holy One, blessed be He, above — these are the head-tefillin. The arm-tefillin have four portions; the heart rides, a model of the lower chariot, and the lower one rides. Further, we have learned, this one riding on the arm below, and the heart riding [is] a model of that which is below, and all the hosts of heaven are given into its hand to be answered — likewise the heart rides below, and all the limbs of the body are given into its hand, and above them are the four portions upon the brain of the head — but the Holy One, blessed be He, is the supernal ruler, King over all. And the mystery of this wisdom is in the manner of the sanctuary, as it is written, "and make one cherub on one end, and one cherub on the other end" (Exodus 25:19), and above them the King's dwelling is in four letters, two chariots; and in this manner heart and brain, heart on one side and brain on the other, and above them is the dwelling of the Holy One, blessed be He, in the four, the four portions. Rabbi Elazar said, from here onward is the mystery of the crowns of the letters, and the portions themselves, and their straps, given as a law to Moses at Sinai, and their hint is revealed, and the reason for it all is in the thirteen attributes of mercy. Rabbi Yehudah said, even had I come only for the sake of this mystery, it would have sufficed — so far his words. This passage makes clear that tefillin are vessels for causing the Shechinah to rest upon us, for they are a model of the supernal cherubim upon whom the Shechinah rested.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:64: And they said in the Midrash (Shocher Tov, Psalms 1): Rabbi Eliezer said, Israel said before the Omnipresent, "We wish to toil in Torah day and night, but we have no leisure." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, "Fulfill the commandment of tefillin, and I will account it to you as though you toil in it day and night." Rabbi Yochanan said, it is an explicit verse: "and it shall be for a sign upon your hand... that the Torah of the Lord may be in your mouth" (Exodus 13:9) — so far his words. This shows that the merit of one who wears tefillin is as great as one who is occupied with Torah; and it is known that Torah study is equal to all the commandments, as it says (Pe'ah 1:1), "and Torah study is equal to them all." And likewise the commandment of tzitzit is equal to them all, as explained, of blessed memory (Nedarim 25a); it follows that one who wraps himself in tzitzit and wears tefillin is as though he had fulfilled all the commandments.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:65: And so it says in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 101b), in these words: the Holy Lamp [Rashbi] said, whoever wears tefillin and tzitzit is as though he had fulfilled the 613 commandments of the Torah; and not only that, but through tzitzit it is as though he established a throne for the Holy One, blessed be He, and the tefillin are the Name of the Lord (Shem YHVH), as though YHVH had descended upon the Throne — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:66: And in the Tikkunim (2a) it says that a person must have, every single day, two signs — the sign of the Covenant [circumcision] and the sign of tefillin — corresponding to the two Yods in the Name YAHDONHY, and on Shabbat, the sign of Shabbat and the sign of the Covenant. And whoever does not don tefillin every day causes separation — we quoted this passage in the Gate of Love (ch. 9): as long as tefillin are upon a person, he effects the unification of the two Names, and the Shechinah rests upon him, for the tefillin are on her side.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:67: And so Rabbi Moshe of Coucy wrote (Semag, positive commandments 3), regarding tefillin, in these words: I further taught them that of the six hundred thirteen commandments given to Israel, there is no commandment that serves as a sign and testimony except three commandments: circumcision, Shabbat, and tefillin, in all three of which the word "sign" (ot) is written; and all three are a sign and testimony for Israel that they are servants of the Holy One, blessed be He — and "by the mouth of two witnesses a matter is established." Each Jew is not a complete Jew unless he has two witnesses that he is a Jew. Therefore, on Sabbaths and festivals, which are called "Shabbat," and Shabbat is called "a sign," a person is exempt from wearing tefillin, since it is enough for him that he has two witnesses that he is a Jew — the testimony of Shabbat and the testimony of circumcision — but on weekdays, every person is obligated to wear tefillin, so that he may have two witnesses, the sign of tefillin along with the sign of circumcision; and whoever does not wear tefillin has only one witness that he is a Jew, and is therefore considered like one under a ban from Heaven (Pesachim 113b). And should you ask, since tefillin are a sign and testimony like circumcision and Shabbat, why has it become lax in the hands of Israel? Our Rabbis have already explained this matter: any matter of a commandment for which they did not give their lives in a time of persecution remains lax in their hands — such as tefillin.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:68: And since all three of these are a sign and testimony, each of them was weighed as equal to the whole Torah — for regarding circumcision, thirteen covenants were established over it, [and] in the Torah, three covenants; and Torah, tefillin, and Shabbat are equated together in several places, one of them (cf. Nehemiah 9:14): "and You gave them Torah and commandments and Your holy Sabbath You made known to them," and regarding tefillin (Exodus 13:9): "that the Torah of the Lord may be in your mouth."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:69: I further taught them: that our Rabbis said (Shabbat 49a) that tefillin require a clean body, like Elisha "the man of wings," that one not sleep or pass wind while wearing them — this refers to a person who wears them all day as their mitzvah requires, lest he forget them upon himself and do something improper; but at the time of prayer, there is no wicked person unfit for tefillin — an a fortiori argument from a Torah scroll, which is more sanctified, containing the whole Torah, whereas tefillin contain only four passages within a piece of leather — and everyone holds a Torah scroll at the time of prayer, since everyone is able to conduct themselves with purity at the time of prayer.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:70: And I further brought to them what our Rabbis expounded (Bechorot 5a): why is it stated, "And it shall be when [the Lord] brings you [into the land]" (Exodus 13:11), in the portion of tefillin? For tefillin are an obligation of the body, observed both in the Land and outside the Land. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, said, perform this mitzvah, for through it you shall merit to enter the Land. Further, our Rabbis said (Menachot 44a), whoever does not wear tefillin transgresses eight positive commandments every day, for there are four portions [in the tefillin], and in each there is a positive commandment of the hand and a positive commandment of the head. Further, our Rabbis said (Berachot 14b), whoever recites the Shema without tefillin is as though he testifies false testimony against himself. Further, our Rabbis said (Rosh Hashanah 17a), the transgressors of Israel in their bodies are judged for twelve months in Gehinnom, [including] the "skull" (karkafta) who never wore tefillin — meaning the skull, that is, the head. Rabbeinu Yaakov explains this as one who abstained from tefillin out of rebellion and contempt for the mitzvah, as it says in Yoma (36b), "transgressions" (pesha'im) refers to acts of rebellion. And Rav Alfasi (the Rif) explains it as one who never wore tefillin [at all, even accidentally]. There is a difficulty with his words, for he should have said "one who did not don tefillin" [in the passive]. Neither has certainty that his interpretation is correct, and therefore one should be careful.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:71: I further taught them, that the Holy One, blessed be He, desires more that a wicked person wear tefillin than a righteous one, for the essential purpose of tefillin's commandment is to be a remembrance for the wicked, to set them straight on a good path, and they need remembrance and strengthening more than those who have grown up in the fear of Heaven all their days. And I brought a great and strong proof: that in the tefillin there are four portions, and in each is written "totafot," except for one where the verse changes and writes instead "and for a remembrance" — teaching that the essential obligation of tefillin is for those who need more remembrance.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:72: Further, our Rabbis said (Menachot 43a): whoever has tefillin on his head and arm, and tzitzit on his garment, and a mezuzah on his doorpost, is presumed not to sin, as it is said, "and a threefold cord is not quickly broken" (Ecclesiastes 4:12), and it says, "The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him and delivers them" (Psalms 34:8) — meaning that "angel" refers to the commandments of God, which encamp around him and remind him of the service of the Creator. And so we find there (44a) regarding a certain man who was kept from a great transgression by his tzitzit, which he saw and was reminded through. Further, our Rabbis said (Menachot, ibid.), whoever wears tefillin lives long, as it says, "the Lord is upon them, they shall live" (Isaiah 38:16, as read homiletically).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:73: And further, in the Tikkunim (2a), a person needs, every single day, two signs, the sign of circumcision and the sign of tefillin, in order to unify the Name YAHDONHY; and on Shabbat, the sign of Shabbat and the sign of circumcision — we quoted this passage in the Gate of Love (ch. 9). It follows that as long as tefillin are upon him he performs the unification, and the Shechinah rests upon him, since the tefillin are on her side.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:74: Further, in the Tikkunim (end of 142b), it says that one who occupies himself with Torah while wrapped in tzitzit and tefillin merits nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, in these words: and therefore Israel need to illuminate her (the Shechinah) in exile with light and a lamp, which is Torah and the mitzvot — the light of the neshamah, nefesh and ruach, which spell the sign "ner" (lamp), within the boxes of tefillin, to find in them the Shechinah in exile, and the covering of tzitzit to be wrapped in it. Therefore, if a person does not don tefillin and tzitzit, with what shall she [the Shechinah] lie in exile? Concerning her it is said, "Fortunate is he who considers the poor; the Lord shall deliver him in the day of evil" (Psalms 41:2). And by the merit of these commandments, people inherit the three knots, which are neshamah, ruach, and nefesh. And it further says there, therefore neshamah, ruach, and nefesh are the bedding of the Shechinah in exile, and concerning them it is said, "and he shall sleep in his garment and bless you" (Deuteronomy 24:13), and by the merit of these commandments the Shechinah rests upon a person.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:75: This passage makes clear that these three commandments — Torah, tefillin, and tzitzit — correspond to neshamah, ruach, and nefesh, as explained at the beginning of the passage, where it says, "the light of the neshamah." Torah, too, is among the commandments, being one of the two hundred forty-eight positive commandments, to study Torah, and so on; and once he merits these three, the Shechinah rests upon him, for the Shechinah rests only upon a complete throne, which is these three, as explained at the end of the passage. It is certainly for this reason that it was the practice of the early Tannaim to wear tefillin all day, as I proved above, in order to draw the Shechinah upon themselves through being a complete throne, as explained in the passage.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:76: And so it is also said (Berachot 30b): Rabbi Yirmiyah was sitting before Rabbi Zeira; he saw that he was very cheerful. He said to him, "Does the master not hold that 'in all sorrow there is profit' (Proverbs 14:23)?" (Rashi explains: when a person shows himself sorrowful, he has reward.) He said to him, "I am wearing tefillin" (Rashi explains: "I am wearing tefillin" — they are testimony that the dominion and kingship of my Master is upon me). It is difficult to say that this donning of tefillin was during the time of prayer, since Rabbi Yirmiyah's statement, "was sitting before Rabbi Zeira," suggests it was in the study hall, not at the time of prayer. And according to the reading of Rabbeinu Yonah, of blessed memory, which reads just before this, regarding Abaye, "was sitting before Rava; he saw that he was very cheerful. He said to him, 'It is written, "and rejoice with trembling"' (Psalms 2:11). He said to him, 'I am wearing tefillin.'" It seems certain that this was not at the time of prayer; for if it were the time of prayer, this would be very difficult for these Amoraim, for could the Mishnah (Berachot 5:1), "One should not stand to pray except in a solemn frame of mind," have been forgotten by them? And likewise, Rabbi Zeira did not say to Rabbi Yirmiyah, "It is written, 'and rejoice with trembling,'" for that verse is more clearly indicative of the matter of prayer, since it was from this very verse that the Gemara above derived that one should not stand to pray except in a solemn frame of mind, more than from the verse "in all sorrow there is profit." And likewise, Rabbi Zeira and Rava did not say, "Have we not learned, one should not stand to pray except in a solemn frame of mind?" Rather, certainly it does not speak of the time of prayer, for their practice was to wear tefillin all day, even while occupied with Torah study.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:77: Regarding what each one answered, "I am wearing tefillin," the students of Rabbeinu Yonah explained, in these words: he means, "I rejoice in the joy of a mitzvah, for I was ill in my bowels and was unable to wear tefillin for these several days out of concern for cleanliness, and now that I have recovered, I rejoice in fulfilling this mitzvah, out of my desire for it" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:78: Further, we say in the Gemara (Berachot 23b): Rabbi Yitzchak said, one who enters a fixed feast removes his tefillin and then enters — and this disagrees with Rabbi Chiya, for Rabbi Chiya said, he places them on his table, and so they are proper for him. And until when? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said, until the time of the [Grace after Meals] blessing. Rashi explains: "removes his tefillin" lest he become drunk at the feast and disgrace himself while wearing tefillin. "And so they are proper for him" — that they be ready for him, and he puts them back on at the time of the blessing — so far his words. And Rabbeinu Yaakov (the Tur, Orach Chaim, siman 40) ruled like Rabbi Chiya. And the Rif, of blessed memory: one who enters a fixed feast removes them and places them on the table until the time of the blessing, and puts them back on — so far his words. Therefore a person should accustom himself to this mitzvah of tefillin, to wear them most of the day, and he will merit length of days. Nevertheless, one who wears tefillin all day and studies Torah while wearing them must handle them constantly, so that his mind not stray from them — for our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Menachot 36b), an a fortiori argument from the frontplate (tzitz), which contained only one mention [of the Divine Name], and so on; how much more so tefillin, which contain forty-two [mentions].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:79: And if it is impossible for a person to wear them throughout the day because of concern for his body's cleanliness, at least at the time of prayer he should wear them, for at the time of prayer one should pray with a clean body — since it is forbidden for him to pray if he cannot hold himself for the duration of walking a parsah [without relieving himself], as explained in the Gemara — and since his body is clean enough for prayer, it is likewise clean enough for tefillin.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:80: And they explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 108b) that the completeness of prayer is in wrapping oneself in tallit and tefillin, in these words: and if the prayer is to ascend complete, through the wrapping of the mitzvah and tefillin upon the head and arm, then it is said of them, "and all the peoples of the earth shall see that the Name of the Lord is called upon you, and they shall fear you" (Deuteronomy 28:10) — "the Name of the Lord" is established as referring to the head-tefillin, and whoever sees the Name of the Lord upon the head during prayer, which is the Name YHVH, immediately all [the harmful forces] flee — this is what is written, "A thousand shall fall at your side..." (Psalms 91:7) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:81: Further, in the Zohar (Parashat Toldot 141a), in these words: and therefore, whoever does not wrap himself in this, and is not crowned to be strengthened by the tefillin every day, it is as though faith does not rest with him, and the fear of his Master is removed from him, and his prayer is not a proper prayer — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:82: Therefore it is fitting that every prayer be recited while wrapped in tzitzit and tefillin, except for the evening prayer; and already the practice has spread in the Land of Israel to wear tefillin even during the afternoon prayer (Minchah). This is a fitting practice, because the special property of tefillin is to subdue the external forces, as explained in the passage; and this is one of the intentions that Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains in the Tikkunim, that one who intends [properly] should intend, at the time of donning tefillin, to subdue the servant beneath his master and the maidservant beneath her mistress. And so it is explained in the Tikkunim (2a), in these words: "mighty ones" from the side of Gevurah, who give strength to their masters, to subdue the servant beneath his master and the maidservant beneath her mistress, through the knot of the tefillin — for whoever does not have tefillin at the time of reciting the Shema, from his side the servant and maidservant rule over the world, and at that hour the Shechinah is angered — this is what is written, "under a servant when he reigns, and a maidservant when she supplants her mistress" (Proverbs 30:22) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:83: And in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, it says regarding the verse, "and Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him" (Genesis 32:24), our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said: this teaches that he wished to kill him, but had no power, because our father Jacob was armed with tefillin on his head and arm and tzitzit on his garment — this is what is written, "And when he saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched..." (Genesis 32:25), and so on. It is known that this "man" was the guardian angel (sar) of Persia, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:84: And in the Tikkunim, elsewhere, found in our possession in manuscript (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 106b), the matter is explained further, drawing a distinction between a servant and a son in the performance of this mitzvah, in these words: whoever's neshamah is from the Tree of Life, certainly, when he dons tefillin, is to bring all other gods under the entire dominion of the supernal Shechinah, which is the head-tefillah of a person, and to bring all nations under the hand of the Lord, which is the lower Shechinah — because in exile it is said, "For three things the earth is disquieted... under a servant when he reigns, and a churl (naval) when he is filled with food, and a maidservant when she supplants her mistress" (Proverbs 30:21-23). Therefore, through the head and hand tefillin, [the intent is] to bring the maidservant under her supernal and lower mistress; and in the mentions [of the Name] within, which are contained in them, corresponding to the Torah, one must bring the servant under his supernal and lower master. This is called "the son of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah" — this is what is written, "Thus says the Lord, Israel is My son, My firstborn" (Exodus 4:22); and those who do this, of them it is said, "You are children to the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 14:1). And therefore it is said (Avot 1:3), "Do not be like servants who serve their master in order to receive a reward." And whoever performs this commandment in order to bind other gods to be subjugated, and the nations below to be placed beneath his hand, they give him a neshamah only from the side of a servant; therefore [it may be] whether as sons or as servants — so far his words. And what it says, "beneath her supernal and lower mistress," refers to the supernal Heh and the lower Heh; and "beneath his supernal and lower master" refers to Yod and Vav.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:85: This passage makes clear the intent of tefillin in one manner, and the distinction in performing this mitzvah between a servant and a son — for the son does not intend his own benefit, but only what pertains to the honor of his father and mother, and therefore intends the subjugation of the kelipot, the servant beneath his master and the maidservant beneath her mistress.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:86: Further, it is explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 101b) that tefillin, for the intermediate ones (beinonim), have the special property of subduing the accusers (mekatregim). It says there, regarding the distinction in the performance of the commandments of tzitzit and tefillin between the fully righteous and the intermediate: that the righteous intend to establish a throne for the King through the wrapping of tzitzit, and for the King to come and sit upon the throne through the donning of tefillin, as explained above; and it says that from the side of the fully righteous, he is not imprisoned in exile, but is bound and imprisoned with them out of love, tied to them in affection — this is what is written, "and his soul is bound up with his soul" (Genesis 44:30) — imprisoned with them in the Throne that they establish for Him and in her Chariot, and so on; but from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil, which binds them with the good inclination to be a help alongside them, and binds them with the evil inclination to be a burden beneath them, [like] a donkey carrying books. From the side of the intermediate ones, he is bound and imprisoned in exile, of whom it is said, on weekdays he was bound like an ox for plowing and like a donkey for burden, and on Shabbat, "that your ox and your donkey may rest" (Exodus 23:12) — he was like an ox for the yoke — the yoke of tefillin — and like a donkey for burden. Of the wicked it is said, "The Lord has given me into the hands of those I cannot withstand" (Lamentations 1:14) — for the straps of the tefillin are like ropes for the horns of Samael, the goring ox that is not destroyed, and the hand-tefillah is bound to his legs; and whoever does not don tefillin, of him it is said (Berachot 33a), "keep far from a goring ox as far as your eyes can see" — for from him depend the primary categories of damage; tzitzit is a burden upon the donkey — so far his words.
